summary: Deep dive on autoscaling behavior, capacity planning and burst policies for QuantaHealth's low-latency inference workloads. Discussed queueing models, reserved GPUs vs burst capacity, KV cache hit-rate impact, batching and quantization tradeoffs, and network constraints for VPC/on-prem deployments. Agreed next steps: sizing worksheet, sample traces, benchmark run, and security docs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park, Marco Ruiz, Samir Patel (Redwood); Aisha Khan, Ben Caldwell, Dr. Priya Menon, Rita Gomez, Marcus Lee (QuantaHealth)

Auto sections: Summary: brief at top; Action items: noted in next steps; Topics: autoscaling, KV cache, batching.

[00:00] Lena (Redwood): hey everyone thanks for carving out the time; quick roll call, we got Aisha, Ben?
[00:07] Aisha (QuantaHealth): yeah hi, here. sorry I'm a few minutes late, got pulled into an admin thing.
[00:12] Marco (Redwood SE): no worries, we can start with context. we'll aim to cover queueing models, burst policies, reserved GPUs, and the on-prem/VPC constraints you mentioned.
[00:24] Ben (QuantaHealth): great, our main ask is consistent p95 latency under 200ms for chat completions at peak of around 350 qps for critical flows. non-critical flows can be relaxed.
[00:34] Samir (Redwood): ok that helps. is that 350 qps mix weighted by short prompts or long prompts? sequence length distribution matters a lot for KV cache and batching.
[00:43] Priya (QuantaHealth): majority are short — typically 50-150 tokens. but we have a long-tail where some batch jobs hit 2k tokens.
[00:51] Lena: okay so short interactive traffic, with occasional long tails. are you planning to host in VPC or want an on-prem rack?
[00:58] Aisha: primary is VPC in our cloud region, but for PHI regulation in a couple of hospitals we need an on-prem option later this year.
[01:06] Marco: good to know. that'll impact autoscaling because on-prem capacity is finite; we can do a hybrid routing policy — hosted for most, on-prem reserved pools for PHI.
[01:16] Marcus (QuantaHealth SRE): question — how does Redwood handle bursts? we have sudden spikes from scheduled processing windows. we can't overprovision too much.
[01:24] Marco: we support burst policies via two levers: reserved GPU pools and a shared burst pool service. reserved GPUs give deterministic throughput; burst pools let you exceed reserved capacity by queuing and/or temporary borrowing from a shared capacity lane with higher cost.
[01:38] Ben: what's the queueing model when burst kicks in? do you prefer queueing requests or dropping them?
[01:44] Samir: default is adaptive queueing with backpressure. small queue up to a configurable max (we recommend 200–500 concurrent request slots per pool), with priority routing for critical flows. when queue length + estimated wait exceeds your p95 SLO we route to fallback models or reject with a soft-fail—return a best-effort cached response.
[02:02] Priya: can you explain estimated wait — is it based on tokens in the batch or measured GPU throughput?
[02:08] Marco: both. runtime maintains a moving average of per-token throughput per model variant plus current in-flight batch formations. estimated latency = kv-cache-hit-adjusted token count / throughput + queue serialization overhead. note — KV cache hits can reduce token work substantially for conversational sessions.
[02:26] Aisha: about KV cache — we heard performance gains are large but cache hit rate depends on session affinity and tokenization. how do you recommend sizing for that?
[02:34] Marco: absolutely. for short interactive agents with session affinity, you'll commonly see 60–85% KV cache hit rates if you keep sessions pinned and have reasonable prefix reuse. we recommend reserving RAM for KV cache per GPU and configuring session timeouts aligned with user sessions. if you can't pin, hit rates drop to 20–40% which drastically increases tail latency.
[02:54] Ben: what are practical numbers — e.g., for one A100 equivalent, what qps can we sustain at 70% hits and average 100 tokens?
[03:03] Samir: rough ballpark: a single A100-class GPU with optimizations and quantized model can handle ~400–800 token-generation qps for 100-token responses if batching is tuned; with 70% kv hits effective token work is maybe 30 tokens average, so throughput scales accordingly. but real numbers depend on model, quantization (4-bit vs 8-bit), and attention optimizations.
[03:22] Priya: we plan to use Llama-3-13B quantized — any pitfalls?
[03:27] Marco: 13B quantized to 4-bit (q4) gives good cost/latency tradeoffs but watch for quality regressions on safety-critical prompts; also memory layout for KV cache changes with quantization — some runtimes need more scratch space. we can recommend per-model profiles.
[03:44] Aisha: on autoscaling triggers — should we rely on GPU utilization or queue length? we see noisy GPU metrics in our infra.
[03:51] Lena: good question — we recommend multi-signal policies: primary on short-term queue length and p95 observed latency, secondary on GPU utilization. queue length correlates directly with user-facing latency, GPU util can be noisy due to batching dynamics.
[04:05] Marcus: how fast can you spin up reserved GPUs? in our on-prem case spin up is manual, cloud is faster.
[04:11] Marco: in hosted/cloud we support warm pools and node prewarming so scale-up can be under 90s for additional shards in many regions. reserved capacity (dedicated GPUs) is instant because it's pre-allocated. on-prem depends on your orchestration — we can integrate with your cluster autoscaler but expect minutes to tens of minutes for physical provisioning.
[04:29] Ben: are prewarmed nodes billed differently?
[04:32] Samir: yes, warm nodes in burst pool have a higher per-minute cost because they reserve memory and keep model caches hot. we include cost telemetry so you can see $/inference during burst windows.
[04:42] Priya: queueing and batching — how do you balance batch size vs latency? our workload is latency-sensitive so large batches might be harmful.
[04:50] Marco: we use dynamic batching heuristics: if p50 vs p95 latency budget allows, we grow batch sizes to improve throughput; otherwise we cap max batch and prioritize low-latency flows. there's also continuous batching that forms small minibatches quickly (tens of ms) to get vectorized kernels benefits without adding large latency.
[05:05] Aisha: can you show an example policy?
[05:08] Marco: e.g., for critical flows: max_batch=8, max_wait=20ms; for non-critical: max_batch=64, max_wait=120ms. combined with KV cache hit-aware scoring — if session has high hit-rate we can be more aggressive.
[05:21] Marcus: we have a compliance question — when you burst to shared capacity, is data from PHI workloads ever exposed outside our dedicated pool?
[05:29] Lena: no, for PHI you'd want the on-prem reserved pool option or we can reserve a private burst lane inside your VPC where data remains in your tenancy; shared public burst pools are not acceptable for PHI. we'll mark that as a hard constraint.
[05:41] Rita (Security): likewise, we need KMS integration and audit logs for model requests. what's available?
[05:46] Samir: KMS and HSM integrations available for Private deployments; hosted supports customer-managed keys in many regions. we emit detailed audit logs per request and have SSO/SAML + RBAC. we will send SOC2 and network diagrams after this call.
[05:59] Ben: coming back to capacity planning — if we want a 99th percentile guarantee for critical flows, how many reserved GPUs should we commit to?
[06:07] Marco: we'll need your traffic trace to simulate. rough heuristic: take peak qps for critical flows, multiply by average effective tokens per request (accounting for kv hits), divide by per-GPU sustainable throughput at your latency SLO. add 25% buffer for headroom. we can run a sizing worksheet.
[06:25] Aisha: ok we'll share traces. what's the expected difference in cost between reserved capacity and bursting?
[06:31] Samir: reserved is cheaper per token because it's committed; burst has a premium due to prewarmed nodes and on-demand overhead. typical delta 15–40% depending on utilization.
[06:41] Priya: any guidance on quantization choices? 4-bit saves a lot but sometimes hurts generation stability.
[06:47] Marco: test on your eval prompts — Redwood Optimize can run automatic quantization profiles and measure quality regressions. we recommend trying q4 for internal flows and q5/8 for safety-critical production. we can include that in the pilot.
[06:58] Ben: about queuing models again — can you surface estimated wait times to the caller so we can show a spinner with ETA instead of timeouts?
[07:05] Lena: yes, runtime can return an estimated queue wait in the response headers and provide retry-after semantics. it's best-effort and based on the moving averages Marco mentioned.
[07:13] Marcus: do you support per-route SLOs and per-customer throttles?
[07:18] Marco: yes, Route-level policies with token limits, concurrency limits, and fallback routing. You can have a critical route pinned to reserved GPUs with strict concurrency and a best-effort route that uses burst.
[07:28] Aisha: network — our VPC egress to Redwood hosted endpoints is limited during business hours. for VPC/private we'd prefer direct peering. what's recommended?
[07:36] Samir: direct VPC peering or private link is recommended for low latency and predictable networking. for on-prem we can do a VPN or direct connect; large throughput needs dedicated circuits. we'll need your network diagram to propose bandwidth and NAT/pat mapping.
[07:50] Priya: on metrics — what telemetry do you provide to help us auto-scale?
[07:55] Marco: you get per-route token counts, observed latency distributions (p50/p95/p99), batch sizes, kv-cache hit rates, GPU util, and queue length. You can hook that into your autoscaler or use Redwood's autoscaling policies.
[08:06] Rita: retention of logs — how long are request logs kept and can that be configured?
[08:10] Samir: configurable per-contract. for Private deployments you control retention; hosted has tiers (30/90/365 days) as add-ons.
[08:18] Ben: hypothetical scenario — peak of 500 qps for critical flows for 10 minutes, short prompts 80 tokens, kv hit 65%. how do you size?
[08:27] Marco: calc: effective avg tokens = 80 * (1 - 0.65) = 28 tokens. assume per-GPU throughput at that profile is 1,000 tokens/s for latency target — that equals ~35 reqs/s per GPU => approx 14 GPUs to cover 500 qps; add 25% headroom => ~18 GPUs reserved or mix 12 reserved + burst capacity. we'll run exact numbers with traces.
[08:54] Aisha: that helps. what about cold-cache penalties during scale-up?
[08:59] Samir: cold caches can cause a 2–4x increase in token processing cost for initial requests as KV fills. warm pools mitigate that. we also prewarm common prompts into prefix caches for the first N sessions.
[09:12] Marcus: how do you estimate cost for warm nodes?
[09:16] Samir: warm nodes include memory-reserved costs plus a marginal prewarm fee; you'll see it in the pricing sheet. typically warm pool costs are amortized if you have repeated bursts.
[09:25] Priya: talking about fallback models — you mentioned auto-fallback to smaller models. how transparent is that and does it preserve context?
[09:32] Marco: fallback policies can be model-based (e.g., route to 7B quantized variant) and we can keep session context by forwarding KV cache where compatible; for different architecture models context may need truncation. we log fallback events for analysis.
[09:47] Ben: does fallback require copying data externally?
[09:50] Lena: no, routing happens inside the same tenancy and VPC lanes; data does not leave your environment for Private or VPC flows.
[09:58] Rita: last security question — can we restrict which models are allowed per route?
[10:03] Samir: yes, allowlist models per route and deny fallback to anything outside the allowlist for sensitive routes.
[10:10] Aisha: moving on — what's a recommended pilot scope? we want to validate p95 latency and cost for critical flows and test on-prem routing.
[10:18] Lena: recommended pilot: 2-week run with 1–2 reserved GPUs in your VPC for critical route plus burst enabled, include 48–72 hour benchmark with synthetic replay of peak traffic, and a smaller on-prem cluster test with 1 physical node to validate routing and KMS.
[10:33] Marcus: we'll need a runbook for the benchmark — can Redwood run it or do we run locally?
[10:37] Marco: Redwood can run the benchmark remotely if you provide traces and network access; we can also run a joint test with your SREs.
[10:44] Priya: how do we measure quality regressions from quant? is there tooling?
[10:48] Samir: Redwood Optimize has eval harnesses — you give a validation prompt set and it runs regression tests across model/quant pairs and produces diffs and quality metrics.
[10:56] Ben: any gotchas for VPC private endpoints and TLS termination?
[10:59] Marco: be mindful of mutual TLS for private link; TLS termination options depend on the deployment mode — Private deployments give you full control. also ensure MTU and jumbo frame settings on direct connects to avoid fragmentation on large messages.
[11:12] Aisha: timeline — we want a pilot start by end of month. is that feasible?
[11:16] Lena: yes if we get traces and the sizing worksheet this week, we can provision reserved GPUs and schedule the benchmark the week of April 20th.
[11:25] Marcus: can we get an estimate for required network bandwidth?
[11:29] Samir: we'll calculate from the traces, but rule of thumb: for 500 qps with 100 tokens responses roughly 500 * 100 tokens * average token size ~ 50 bytes => ~2.5 MB/s plus overhead. multiply for concurrency and safety margin. we'll give precise numbers.
[11:44] Priya: one more — are there prebuilt dashboards for cost per route and per-token cost?
[11:48] Marco: yes Redwood Console has per-route cost drilling and anomaly alerts; you can tie alerts to Model Regression or cost spikes.
[11:55] Ben: thanks — this was helpful. let's recap next steps.
[12:00] Lena: recap: Redwood: send sizing worksheet, pricing, SOC2 + security docs, propose benchmark windows. QuantaHealth: share 2 weeks of traces, network diagram, confirm pilot start date. we'll schedule the benchmark follow-up.
[12:14] Aisha: thanks all. any outstanding blockers?
[12:17] Rita: security will re-review SOC2 but that's standard.
[12:20] Lena: perfect; we'll follow up in email. thanks everyone.

End of transcript.
